claims.claim: In 2024, Stonehenge's Altar Stone was traced to Scotland.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 (Clarke et al., Nature 632, 570-575; online 14 Aug 2024 per Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1). Abstract from Crossref; full text read via the Firecrawl research index (PMC11324516 copy of the article).
claims.note: Title 'A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge'; abstract: detrital ages 'reveal a remarkable similarity to the Old Red Sandstone of the Orcadian Basin in northeast Scotland'; body: 'indicate that the Altar Stone of Stonehenge has a provenance from the ORS in the Orcadian Basin of northeast Scotland'. A viewer who swipes away after this sentence (A4) leaves with a true statement of what the 2024 paper found.

claims.claim: Now nobody can say exactly where it came from.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090 (Pirrie et al., J. Geol. Soc. 183(6), online 5 Nov 2026) and doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 (Clarke et al., J. Quaternary Sci. 41(6), online 4 Jun 2026): ABSTRACTS ONLY, as deposited with Crossref; full texts not reachable (publisher bot challenges, not in the research index).
claims.note: The substance is supported: Pirrie 2026 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'; Clarke 2026 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'. But 'Now' implies the exact source was known in 2024 and has since been lost. Clarke 2024 only ever named a basin (the Orcadian Basin), and Clarke 2026 says the location 'remains' unresolved. Change 'Now nobody can say' to wording of continuity, e.g. 'Exactly where it came from is still unknown' (as the short's own title already says). The A4 hook test passes on sentence 1 alone; this is about sentence 2 overstating a change.

claims.claim: The ages of tiny mineral grains inside it matched sandstone in the northeast.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1, full text via Firecrawl research index (PMC11324516): Abstract, 'Orcadian Basin ORS' section and Methods.
claims.note: U-Pb/Lu-Hf ages of zircon, apatite and rutile grains 'typically 10-40 um wide'; 'The detrital zircon age spectra from Orcadian Basin ORS provides the closest match'; KS test cannot distinguish them; apatite age components from Spittal (Caithness) and Cruaday (Orkney) 'match those from the Altar Stone'. 'Matched' is fair for this; 'the northeast' follows 'Scotland' in the previous sentence.

claims.claim: If so, how did six tonnes travel more than seven hundred kilometres?
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 abstract (Crossref) and full text (research index); doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 abstract (Crossref).
claims.note: Clarke 2024: 'a 6 tonne shaped block, was sourced at least 750 km from its current location'; body: 'measuring 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m ... weighing 6 t'; 'a Scottish provenance ... demands a transport distance of at least 750 km'. Clarke 2026: '6000 kg', 'some 700 km'. 'More than seven hundred' sits under both; 'If so' keeps the condition on the Scottish source.

claims.claim: The 2024 team suggested it went by sea.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 abstract (Crossref) and full text (research index).
claims.note: Abstract: 'The difficulty of long-distance overland transport ... suggests that it was transported by sea.' Body: the geography 'would have permitted sea routes southward from the Orcadian Basin towards southern England'.

claims.claim: But no late Stone Age boat has been found in Britain,
claims.source_checked: doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 (Parker Pearson et al., Archaeology International 27(1)): Crossref record read (no abstract deposited). Full text NOT reached: journals.uclpress.co.uk article page and PDF galley both return an Anubis bot challenge; not in the Firecrawl research index; discovery.ucl.ac.uk and research.aber.ac.uk do not resolve in this sandbox.
claims.note: The cited passage ('no boats are known from the Late Neolithic in Britain or Europe'; Ferriby 3 earliest) could not be read. Clarke 2024 does not state it. Needs a reader who can open the Archaeology International text (or allow discovery.ucl.ac.uk). Also note for that check: 'Late Stone Age' is a term of art in African archaeology; lowercase 'late Stone Age' for Late Neolithic is a reasonable plain rendering.

claims.claim: and another study doubts one could carry six tonnes.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13: Crossref metadata only (authors Parker Pearson, Bevins, Bradley, Ixer, Pearce, Richards). Full text not reachable (see claim 6).
claims.note: The 'unlikely to be sturdy enough to carry a 6-tonne stone' wording could not be checked. From Crossref: three of its six authors (Bevins, Ixer, Pearce) are also authors of Clarke 2024, so 'another study' is accurate but it is not an independent team; the SOURCES block already records this.

claims.claim: Overland, on a sledge, that study estimates about eight months of hauling.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13: full text not reachable (see claim 6).
claims.note: The sledge-on-rails description and the 'eight months or so' estimate could not be read in the source. Clarke 2024 (read) discusses overland obstacles but gives no duration.

claims.claim: A glacier? A 2026 ice model says ice could have carried it part of the way, at most.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1002/jqs.70080, ABSTRACT ONLY (Crossref deposit; online 4 Jun 2026). Wiley full text not reachable.
claims.note: Abstract: 'we combine sandstone provenance analysis with ice flow modelling'; 'Glacial dispersal to Dogger Bank would reduce the anthropogenic transport distance ... from 700 km to 400 km'; 'Glacial transport may have provided an intermediate stage in the stone's journey, but alone cannot account for the final emplacement'; 'substantial anthropogenic transport would have remained necessary'. 'Part of the way, at most' matches. The abstract also raises a timing problem (Dogger Bank flooded before the stone likely arrived), which only weakens the idea further, so omitting it does not overstate.

claims.claim: Then, months later, a new study, including three of the 2024 team,
claims.source_checked: Crossref records api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 and /10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 and /10.1002/jqs.70080.
claims.note: Pirrie 2026 published online 5 Nov 2026, about five months after Clarke 2026 (4 Jun 2026). Its authors include Richard E. Bevins, Rob A. Ixer and Nick J. G. Pearce, all three authors of Clarke 2024.

claims.claim: looked closer.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090, ABSTRACT ONLY (Crossref).
claims.note: Abstract: 'a detailed multi-proxy characterization of the sedimentology, geochemistry, detrital and diagenetic mineralogy of the Altar Stone'.

claims.claim: Many outcrops in that part of Scotland could not have been the source.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090, ABSTRACT ONLY (Crossref).
claims.note: Abstract: 'many outcrops of the Old Red Sandstone (ORS) in the Orcadian Basin could not have been the source of the Altar Stone'. 'That part of Scotland' = the northeast / Orcadian Basin named earlier.

claims.claim: No outcrop examined so far has been shown to match it in every way.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090, ABSTRACT ONLY (Crossref).
claims.note: Abstract: 'To date, no examined outcrop area of the UK ORS can be shown to have the same suite of lithological and geochemical characteristics as documented for the Altar Stone.' 'In every way' = 'the same suite'; it does not deny the grain-age match, which the same abstract says still 'supports a Laurentian source'.

claims.claim: Photo of Stonehenge at sunrise, credited 'Photo: Stonehenge Stone Circle (Flickr), CC BY 2.0'
claims.source_checked: public/img/stonehenge-red-sky.jpg viewed (it is Stonehenge silhouetted against a sunrise sky); public/SOURCES.json entry read. The Flickr page and the Commons file page were not opened (this sandbox's network blocks further hosts).
claims.note: The picture matches its description. The credit line and the CC BY 2.0 licence could not be checked against the Flickr/Commons page in this pass; SOURCES.json says the licence was read from Commons on 2026-11-18. Confirm on the file page (D1) before approval. The photo makes no claim about the Altar Stone itself.

claims.claim: Map of Britain (Natural Earth coastlines) with a pin 'Stonehenge' at 51.179 N, 1.826 W
claims.source_checked: src/shorts/altar-stone/map.tsx read. No cited source for the coordinate in the SOURCES block; none opened.
claims.note: The position is the widely published one and an error would be invisible at this map scale, but the SOURCES block cites nothing for it and this pass could not open a citable record (e.g. the Historic England list entry or an Ordnance Survey grid reference). Add one to SOURCES; low risk.

claims.claim: Dashed ellipse around NE Scotland (centre 58.3 N, 3.4 W; ~1.15 deg lon x 0.85 deg lat), line from Stonehenge, tag 'TRACED HERE' / '2024 · NE Scotland'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 full text (research index); src/shorts/altar-stone/index.tsx and map.tsx read.
claims.note: Clarke 2024 traces the stone to the Orcadian Basin, which it describes as including Caithness, Orkney and Shetland ('around 4 km thick in Caithness and up to around 8 km thick in Shetland'). The ellipse spans about 57.45-59.15 N, so it covers both 2024 comparison samples (Spittal 58.47 N, Cruaday 59.08 N) but leaves out Shetland. Under a 'TRACED HERE' tag that draws the traced area smaller and sharper than the paper did. The hook tag also lacks the 'area approx.' note that the later AGES MATCH tag carries. Fix: add 'area approx.' (or 'Orcadian Basin, approx.') to this tag, and either extend the marker to Shetland or say on screen that it is approximate.

claims.claim: '?' over the ellipse; tag 'EXACT SOURCE' / 'unknown'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090 and doi:10.1002/jqs.70080, ABSTRACTS ONLY (Crossref).
claims.note: Pirrie 2026: 'the exact provenance of the Altar Stone is as yet unknown'; Clarke 2026: 'its source location within this large basin remains unresolved'.

claims.claim: Drawn microscope view of sandstone with a few grains highlighted; tag 'MINERAL GRAINS' / '10–40 µm wide' / 'illustration'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 Methods (research index); src/shorts/altar-stone/shots.tsx read.
claims.note: The figure is in the source: 'grains typically 10-40 um wide' (dated targets 'usually <30 um'). But in the drawing the highlighted (dated) grains are copies of ordinary framework grains, the same size as the sand around them, and are scattered. In the source they are heavy minerals (zircon, apatite, rutile) much smaller than the framework grains (mean grain size up to 300 um) and concentrated in 100-200 um heavy-mineral bands. Next to a '10-40 um' label, the picture suggests the whole sandstone is made of grains that size. Fix: draw the highlighted grains a fraction of the framework size (ideally in a band), or add 'not to scale' to the sub-label; 'typically 10–40 µm' would also match the source exactly.

claims.claim: Tag 'AGES MATCH' / 'sandstone of NE Scotland (area approx.)'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 abstract and full text.
claims.note: As claim 3; the approximate area is labelled as such.

claims.claim: Tag '6 TONNES'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 abstract and body; doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 abstract.
claims.note: 'a 6 tonne shaped block'; 'weighing 6 t'; '6000 kg'.

claims.claim: Dashed straight line NE Scotland marker to Stonehenge; tag '700+ KM' / 'if from NE Scotland'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 abstract and body; doi:10.1002/jqs.70080 abstract; line endpoints from index.tsx/map.tsx.
claims.note: Sources: 'at least 750 km' (Clarke 2024), 'some 700 km' (Clarke 2026), both conditional on an Orcadian Basin source, which the sub-label keeps. The drawn line (58.3 N 3.4 W to 51.179 N 1.826 W) is about 800 km great-circle, consistent with '700+'.

claims.claim: Two dashed sea routes (east coast and west coast) to the south coast; tag 'BY SEA?' / 'route not known'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 abstract and body (research index). Fig. 4a itself not viewed.
claims.note: Clarke 2024 argues for sea transport and says the geography 'would have permitted sea routes southward from the Orcadian Basin towards southern England' without naming one; drawing both coasts, dashed, under 'route not known' says no more than that.

claims.claim: Dashed outline of a boat carrying a slab, '?'; tags 'NO BOAT FOUND' / 'from the late Stone Age, in Britain' and 'A 2024 STUDY' / 'boats of the time: unlikely to carry six tonnes'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13: Crossref record only; full text not reachable (see claim 6).
claims.note: Both tags rest on Parker Pearson 2024, which could not be read. Also: Crossref gives this article published-online and issued 2025-01-22 (vol. 27(1)); the SOURCES block says it was published 31 Dec 2024 on the UCL Press page. Confirm the date on the publisher page; if it is 2025, change 'A 2024 STUDY' (and claim 24's '2024 study') to the right year or drop the year.

claims.claim: Hauling scene: rows of people on ropes pulling a slab (4.9 m x 0.5 m to the figures' scale) on a wooden sledge over timber rails; tags '~8 MONTHS' / 'overland estimate, 2024 study' and 'illustration of a hypothesis · crew size not known'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1 body for the dimensions (confirmed: 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m); doi:10.14324/AI.27.1.13 not reachable; haul.tsx read.
claims.note: Slab dimensions are drawn to Clarke 2024's measurements, and the scene is labelled a hypothesis with unknown crew size (A6). But the sledge-on-rails method and the '~8 MONTHS' estimate come from Parker Pearson 2024, which could not be read, and the '2024 study' year conflicts with Crossref's 2025-01-22 date (see claim 23).

claims.claim: Map with a translucent ice sheet labelled 'ice extent illustrative'; stone marker slides along an ice path from NE Scotland to a pin 'Dogger Bank' (54.8 N, 2.0 E), then a dashed line to Stonehenge; tag 'ICE MODEL' / 'part of the way, at most'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1002/jqs.70080, ABSTRACT ONLY (Crossref); index.tsx read.
claims.note: The tag and the shape of the story match the abstract: modelled transport from Caithness 'predominantly towards the north-east, with a localised south-eastward pathway directed towards Dogger Bank', then people the rest of the way. The ice extent is marked illustrative. Not checkable: (a) the Dogger Bank pin position has no cited source; (b) the drawn ice path and the onward route are not labelled illustrative and the paper's modelled path could not be seen (abstract only). Note the abstract gives 400 km from Dogger Bank to Stonehenge, while the drawn pin is about 480 km away, so the pin is probably further from the paper's endpoint than intended. Fix options: source the Dogger Bank point (and move it towards the bank's south-west end if that is what '400 km' measures), and extend the 'illustrative' note to the paths.

claims.claim: Paper card 'Journal of the Geological Society' / '2026' with a magnifier over sandstone; tag 'A NEW STUDY' / 'three of the 2024 team among its authors'
claims.source_checked: Crossref api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/jgs2026-090 and /10.1038/s41586-024-07652-1.
claims.note: Journal of the Geological Society, vol. 183(6), online 5 Nov 2026; Bevins, Ixer and Pearce are authors of both papers. The other lines on the card are grey bars, so no invented text.

claims.claim: Zoomed map of NE Scotland and Orkney with 12 outcrop dots, 9 crossed out in red, 3 left with '?'; tags 'MANY RULED OUT' and 'NO FULL MATCH' / 'shown in any outcrop examined' / 'exact source unknown'; note 'outcrop positions illustrative'
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1144/jgs2026-090, ABSTRACT ONLY (Crossref); index.tsx OUTCROPS array read.
claims.note: The tags match the abstract. The drawing does not: 9 of 12 crossed out, with 3 left as open candidates, reads as data (three-quarters ruled out, a few sites still possible). The abstract gives no counts, does not say any outcrop remains a candidate, and its 'no examined outcrop area of the UK ORS' covers more than the zoomed NE view. The on-screen note covers only positions, not the count or the three survivors. Fix: change the note to 'outcrops illustrative' (count and positions), or drop the '?' survivors; or take the real counts and sites from the full paper.
